opus-5.5.text:
Well, I like to think of computer vision in terms of what I've called the three R's: recognition, reconstruction, and reorganization. Recognition is attaching semantic labels to things: this is a cat, this is a chair, this person is running. Reconstruction is recovering the three-dimensional structure of the world from images: shape, depth, layout. Reorganization is what we used to call perceptual grouping or segmentation: figuring out which pixels go together to form objects and surfaces.

If I look back over my career, progress has been very uneven across these. In recognition, the change in the last decade or so has been dramatic. When I started, recognizing even a handful of object categories reliably in cluttered scenes was a research problem. After deep learning came in, around 2012, performance on benchmarks like ImageNet and then detection on COCO improved enormously, and now we routinely do things that would have seemed like science fiction to me in the 1980s.

Reconstruction has also advanced a great deal, partly through classical geometry, multi-view stereo and structure from motion, and more recently through learning-based methods that can infer 3D shape even from a single image by drawing on prior experience of how the world looks. Reorganization has benefited too; segmentation today is far better than it was.

But I'd add a caution. Benchmarks measure progress on the problems as we've posed them, and that isn't the same as solving vision. A child doesn't learn to see from millions of labeled images. A child learns by moving around, touching things, acting in the world. So the deeper question is whether our systems understand the world in a way that supports action: manipulating objects, navigating, predicting what will happen next. On that front we are much further from human-level competence. That's why I've become increasingly interested in the connection between vision and action, in embodiment, in robotics. Vision evolved in animals to guide behavior, and I think that's ultimately the right yardstick for judging how far we've come.

r001.rationale: The response credits deep learning with major recognition gains, but does not characterize future progress primarily as scaling training data.

r002.rationale: It mentions multi-view stereo and structure from motion as contributors to progress, but does not state that multiple-view 3D reconstruction has very good solutions.

r003.rationale: It says learning-based methods can infer 3D shape from a single image using prior experience, but does not identify substantial unresolved parts of that problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that we've made enormous progress, and the second thing to say is that the problems are not solved. Both of those are true at the same time.

If you go back to when I started in the field, in the early eighties, the core problems were recognition, reconstruction, and reorganization. Recognizing what objects are in the scene, reconstructing the three-dimensional geometry from two-dimensional images, and grouping the pixels into coherent regions, what the Gestalt psychologists called perceptual organization. Those were the problems then, and honestly they're still the problems. What's changed is how far along we are on each of them.

Recognition is where the progress has been most dramatic. In 2012, with the ImageNet moment, we went from systems that could sort of recognize a few categories under constrained conditions to systems that, on standard benchmarks, do as well as or better than humans. And it kept going. Detection, segmentation, pose estimation, these all fell in sequence once the deep learning machinery was in place and the datasets existed. I had been skeptical, I'll admit that. I thought neural networks were something we had tried in the eighties and moved past. I was wrong, and I said so at the time.

Reconstruction, the geometric side, had actually been in reasonably good shape even before deep learning, because there's real mathematics there. Multi-view geometry, structure from motion, these were worked out largely in the nineties and two thousands. What learning added was the ability to do it from a single image, to bring in priors about what shapes in the world look like, and that's been a nice marriage of the two traditions.

But here's where I'd push back on the triumphalism. The benchmarks measure what the benchmarks measure. If you take a system that scores beautifully on ImageNet or COCO and put it on a robot in a kitchen, it falls apart in ways that are quite revealing. It doesn't really understand that objects persist, that they have mass, that a cup is for holding liquid. A two-year-old child knows those things. The child has never seen a labeled dataset. So there's a gap between pattern recognition, which we've gotten very good at, and understanding, which we have not.

I think the honest assessment is that we solved the version of vision that is about mapping images to labels, and we are now confronting the harder version, which is vision in the service of acting in the world. That's why I've moved a lot of my own work toward robotics and embodied agents. Vision evolved in animals so they could move and manipulate and survive, not so they could caption photographs. If we take that seriously, the next set of problems is about learning from interaction, learning with far less supervision, and building representations that support action rather than just classification.

So, enormous progress, no question. But if someone tells you vision is solved, ask them to have their system unload a dishwasher.

r002.rationale: It says the geometric side of reconstruction was in reasonably good shape and specifically cites multi-view geometry and structure from motion as worked-out methods.

r003.rationale: It says learning enabled reconstruction from a single image, but does not identify substantial unresolved parts of that problem.

astra-6.text:
I think we have made tremendous progress, but we have to be precise about which problem we mean. If the question is, “Can you recognize an object in an image?” then the progress has been extraordinary. But recognizing an object is only one part of seeing.

Consider looking at a chair. You can name it, but you also understand its shape, where you could sit, whether it would support you, and how you might move it through a doorway. That involves geometry, physical reasoning, and the relationship between perception and action. A label does not capture all of that.

So I would distinguish progress on particular benchmarks from progress toward the full capability of human vision. The benchmarks tell us something important, but they are not the whole problem. To me, the broader challenge is understanding how vision enables an intelligent agent to act in the world.

r002.rationale: It mentions geometry generally, but does not state that 3D reconstruction has very good solutions when multiple views are available.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have made tremendous progress, but we should be precise about what we mean by progress. If you take image classification—recognizing that an image contains a dog or a car—the improvement has been remarkable. We’ve also made substantial progress in object detection and segmentation: finding objects and identifying which pixels belong to them.

But recognizing objects is only part of seeing. Consider looking at a person reaching for a cup. You understand something about the three-dimensional scene, what the person is trying to do, and what is likely to happen next. That brings in geometry, motion, physical interactions, and intentions. Success on an image recognition benchmark doesn’t establish that a system understands all of that.

So my assessment is that we have solved some very useful pieces, while the broader problem remains open. One particularly interesting direction is connecting vision to action. For a robot, seeing has a purpose: it needs to move through the world and manipulate things. That gives us a much richer test of visual understanding.
